cases.q: How do you monitor a model's performance after deployment
cases.label: strong
cases.answer: I log every prediction with its inputs and, when they arrive later, the true labels, so I can compute live metrics. I watch for data drift by comparing input distributions with the training data, for example with PSI on key features. I compare live precision and recall against the offline baseline and set alerts when they drop more than a threshold. When performance degrades I retrain on recent data, and if a new model is worse I roll back to the previous version.

cases.q: How do you monitor a model's performance after deployment
cases.label: paraphrase
cases.answer: I store what the model predicted for each request and join it later with what actually happened, so quality can be measured in production. I check whether incoming features start to look different from what the model learned on, and I compare live quality numbers with what we measured before launch. If they fall below an agreed level someone gets paged, and we either train again on fresh data or go back to the earlier model version.

cases.q: What makes a REST API well designed
cases.label: strong
cases.answer: Resources are named with plural nouns such as /orders and /orders/42, and the HTTP methods carry the action: GET reads, POST creates, PUT or PATCH updates and DELETE removes, with correct status codes like 201 for created and 404 for not found. Errors use one consistent JSON format with a code and message. Large lists support pagination with limit and offset or cursors, and the API is versioned, for example /v1. Endpoints require authentication with tokens and are documented with OpenAPI.

cases.q: What makes a REST API well designed
cases.label: partial
cases.answer: A good REST API uses GET and POST correctly and returns JSON. It should also be fast.

cases.q: What makes a REST API well designed
cases.label: paraphrase
cases.answer: Each URL names a thing, not an action, like /customers/7, and the verb of the request says what happens to it, while the response number tells the client whether it worked, for instance 201 after creating something or 404 when it doesn't exist. Every failure comes back in the same shape with a code and a readable message. Long collections come in pages, the version sits in the path so old clients keep working, and access needs a token, with an OpenAPI page describing everything.

cases.q: How would you use caching to speed up a slow API endpoint
cases.label: strong
cases.answer: First I measure where the time goes with profiling, because caching the wrong layer does nothing. If the endpoint mostly reads data that rarely changes, I cache the result in Redis with a key that includes every parameter that changes the response, such as the user id and page. I set a TTL and invalidate the entry when the underlying data is updated, so users don't see stale data for long. Afterwards I measure the hit rate and the latency again; in one service this took p95 from 800 ms to 60 ms.

cases.q: How would you use caching to speed up a slow API endpoint
cases.label: paraphrase
cases.answer: Before touching anything I find out which step is actually slow. For data that is read far more often than it changes, I keep a copy of the computed response in an in-memory store, labelled by everything that makes the response differ, like the user and the filters. Copies expire after a set time and are thrown away when the source record changes. Then I check how often requests are served from the copy and whether the response time really dropped.

cases.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread
cases.label: strong
cases.answer: A process has its own separate memory space, so one crashing process does not corrupt another, while threads inside a process share the same memory. Sharing memory makes communication cheap but causes race conditions, so shared data needs locks or other synchronisation. In Python, the GIL means threads help for I/O-bound work like many network calls, while CPU-bound work needs multiple processes. For example, I used a process pool to resize thousands of images and threads to download them.

cases.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread
cases.label: partial
cases.answer: A process is a running program and a thread is a smaller part of it. Threads are lighter than processes.

cases.q: What is the difference between a process and a thread
cases.label: incorrect
cases.answer: Each thread has its own separate memory, so threads can never have race conditions. Processes share memory with each other, which is why they are faster than threads.

cases.q: What problem does Docker solve
cases.label: strong
cases.answer: Docker solves the 'works on my machine' problem by packaging the app with its exact runtime and libraries, so every environment is consistent. I write a Dockerfile that builds an image from a small base image like python:3.12-slim, ordering layers so dependencies are cached and using a multi-stage build to keep it small. For local development I use docker compose to run the API with PostgreSQL and Redis, and secrets are passed as environment variables rather than baked into the image.

cases.label: partial

cases.q: What problem does Docker solve
cases.label: paraphrase
cases.answer: It removes the gap between a developer laptop and the server: the application ships together with the exact runtime and libraries it needs, so it behaves the same everywhere. I describe the build in a recipe file, start from a minimal base, put rarely changing steps first so rebuilds are quick, and use a separate build stage to keep the final artifact small. Locally, one command starts the API together with its database, and passwords come in from the environment instead of being written into the build.
